Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
26-year-old woman with known asthma presents with 2–3-day history of worsening exertional dyspnea, wheeze, and dry cough; clinical picture most consistent with mild asthma exacerbation.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Tight chest, wheeze, dry cough, and shortness of breath that began 2–3 days ago while running; now occurs with brisk walking.  
• Relief measures: Salbutamol (blue inhaler) used several times daily with minimal benefit.  
• Associated symptoms: No sputum, fever, chest pain, or hospital admissions.  
• Asthma control: Previously well-controlled; last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; last nurse review ≈2 years ago. Baseline peak flow ~380 L/min (patient estimate); no recent measurement.  
• Past medical history: Asthma; hay fever; possible eczema.  
• Allergies: No drug allergies reported.  
• Medications:  
  – Salbutamol MDI PRN  
  – Clenil (beclomethasone) 3 puffs BID (patient already on)  
  – Cetraben cream, topical hydrocortisone  
• Family history: Brother—asthma; sister—eczema.  
• Social / preventive: Regular runner; no smoking/alcohol history documented.

Examination:
• Tele-consultation only; no vitals or physical exam performed.  
• No objective peak-flow reading available.

Impression:
Likely mild asthma exacerbation / loss of control.
  – Supported by acute increase in wheeze and SOB, poor response to reliever, known asthma (high likelihood per DDx).  
Alternate considerations (less likely):  
  1. Viral URTI triggering asthma—no systemic viral features.  
  2. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction or poor inhaler technique—initial trigger but now persistent symptoms.

Plan:
• Increase preventer (Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily temporarily.  
• Continue Salbutamol up to every 2 hours as needed; if requiring this frequency or worsening symptoms, proceed to Emergency Department.  
• Arrange face-to-face GP review within the next few days for chest examination, peak-flow assessment, and consideration of oral steroids ± antibiotics.  
• Educate on asthma action plan and importance of regular reviews.  
• No further questions; patient agreed to plan.

Quality checks:
● Missing/expected elements: vitals, objective peak-flow, smoking status, vaccination status, formal allergy list beyond medications, exact follow-up date/time booked.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear but lacks physical exam and some routine history (social habits, vitals).
